dashboard.aiPortfolioSubtitle: Bridgewater All-Weather · grounded on local quant data
dashboard.breadthAdRatioTip: Advance/Decline ratio — how many stocks went up vs down today. >1.5 = strong buying pressure across the board. <0.7 = broad selling. A rising market with falling A/D ratio = bearish divergence (narrow rally, few leaders).
dashboard.breadthInfo: Breadth measures how many stocks participate in a market move. BROAD (>70% above MAs) = healthy, sustainable rally. NARROW (<30%) = weak, only a few stocks leading. Breadth divergences (index rising but breadth falling) are classic warning signals of a coming reversal.
dashboard.breadthNhNlTip: New 20-day Highs minus New 20-day Lows. Positive = more stocks making new highs (bullish). Negative = more stocks making new lows (bearish). Persistent negative readings during a rally = hidden weakness under the surface.
dashboard.breadthPctAbove200Tip: Percentage of stocks above their 200-day moving average. This measures long-term trend health. >65% = broad bull market. <40% = bear market conditions. The 200 DMA is the most-watched MA by institutions — being above it defines an 'uptrend'.
dashboard.breadthPctAbove50Tip: Percentage of S&P 500 stocks trading above their 50-day moving average. This measures short-term momentum. >70% = strong breadth, broad rally. <30% = weak, most stocks in short-term downtrends. Useful for timing: extreme low readings often mark short-term bottoms.
dashboard.cryptoInfo: Live crypto prices from Binance. Momentum is based on 7-day vs 30-day moving average crossover. Bullish = price above both MAs and 7D > 30D. Bearish = price below MAs or 7D < 30D.
dashboard.cycleDescContraction: Slowing growth, rising unemployment, rate cuts
dashboard.cycleDescPeak: Max growth, inflation pressure, rate peak
dashboard.cycleDescTrough: Economic bottom, cheap assets, stimulus begins
dashboard.cycleDetailContraction: GDP decelerates or turns negative. Unemployment rises, earnings disappoint. Central banks pivot to cuts. Bonds and defensives outperform.
dashboard.cycleDetailExpansion: Economy growing above trend. Corporate earnings rise, unemployment falls, central banks tighten. Equities outperform bonds.
dashboard.cycleDetailPeak: Growth at its highest but beginning to slow. Inflation elevated, rates at or near peak. Prefer value/dividend stocks and reduce duration.
dashboard.cycleDetailTrough: Economy at or near bottom. Asset valuations depressed, stimulus underway. Markets price the recovery — strong entry point for equities.
dashboard.cycleInfo: Identifies the current phase of the economic cycle using a Hidden Markov Model on 5 macro indicators (yield curve, unemployment, CPI, industrial production, consumer sentiment). EXPANSION: growth accelerating, buy cyclicals/growth. PEAK: growth slowing, rotate to defensives. CONTRACTION: recession, buy bonds/utilities/staples. TROUGH: recovery starting, buy beaten-down cyclicals — historically the best entry point for equities.
dashboard.cycleModelNote: Model: Gaussian HMM trained on FRED data (T10Y2Y, UNRATE, CPI, INDPRO). States mapped by yield-curve mean.
dashboard.fngTip: Alternative.me Fear & Greed Index for crypto. Combines volatility, volume, social media, BTC dominance, and Google Trends. 0 = Extreme Fear (historically a buy signal). 100 = Extreme Greed (sell signal). A contrarian indicator — be greedy when others are fearful.
dashboard.gexInfo: Gamma Exposure (GEX) measures how much options market-makers (dealers) need to hedge. POSITIVE GEX: dealers sell rallies & buy dips = low volatility, mean-reverting market. NEGATIVE GEX: dealers buy rallies & sell dips = amplified moves, trending/volatile market. This is the #1 intraday regime indicator for SPX/QQQ.
dashboard.gexNetTip: Net Gamma Exposure = Call GEX + Put GEX. Positive = dealers dampen volatility (sell high, buy low). Negative = dealers amplify moves. Large positive = expect tight ranges. Large negative = expect big swings.
dashboard.gexZeroTip: The price level where dealer gamma flips from positive to negative. ABOVE zero-gamma: dealers suppress vol (buy dips). BELOW zero-gamma: dealers amplify selling (sell dips). When SPY drops below this level, expect accelerated selling and higher volatility.
dashboard.inputsMissingNote: {count, plural, one {# input is unavailable — it is not counted in the score} other {# inputs are unavailable — they are not counted in the score}}
dashboard.keySignalsTip: The individual signals driving today's regime assessment, ranked by weight. These are the data points that matter most for risk management right now.
dashboard.macroTapeInfo: Cross-asset macro indicators that provide context for equity positioning. These 6 instruments together tell you about dollar strength, interest rates, inflation expectations, credit stress, and global growth. Divergences between them often signal regime shifts before equities react.
dashboard.macroTipCopper: Copper futures — 'Dr. Copper' has a PhD in economics. Rising copper = global manufacturing expansion. Falling copper = industrial slowdown. One of the most reliable leading indicators of economic activity.
dashboard.macroTipDxy: US Dollar Index — measures USD vs basket of 6 currencies. Rising DXY = tighter financial conditions, headwind for equities and commodities. Falling DXY = easier conditions, tailwind for risk assets and gold.
dashboard.macroTipGold: Gold futures — the ultimate safe haven. Rises during fear, inflation, and USD weakness. Strong gold + weak equities = risk-off regime. Strong gold + strong equities = inflation hedge.
dashboard.macroTipHyg: High Yield Corporate Bond ETF — credit market stress gauge. Falling HYG = credit spreads widening, default risk rising, risk-off. Rising HYG = credit markets calm. HYG often leads equity turns by 1-2 weeks.
dashboard.macroTipOil: WTI Crude Oil — the economic activity barometer. Rising oil = demand strength or supply shock (inflationary). Falling oil = demand destruction (recessionary). Watch for divergence vs equities.
dashboard.macroTipUs10y: 10-Year Treasury Yield — the benchmark risk-free rate. Rising yields = tighter conditions, growth concerns, pressure on growth stocks. Falling yields = flight to safety or easing expectations.

dashboard.sectorRotationInfo: Sector rotation tracks which parts of the economy are leading or lagging. Money flows between sectors based on the business cycle: Early cycle favors Tech & Discretionary, Late cycle favors Energy & Materials, Recession favors Utilities & Staples. The RS Rank shows relative strength (1=strongest). 60D Fwd shows historical average returns for each sector during the current regime.
dashboard.subtitle: Today's read, tuned for short-term & options traders
dashboard.swarmActionBlack: Reduce exposure. Hedging demand high, correlation breakdown.
dashboard.swarmActionGray: Tighten stops. Crowded positioning, momentum fragile.
dashboard.swarmActionNeutral: Mixed signals. Wait for conviction before adding risk.
dashboard.swarmActionWhite: Broad participation. Momentum trades favored, ride the trend.
dashboard.swarmClustersTip: Number of distinct behavioral groups. 0-1 = uniform (herding or collapse). 2-3 = polarized. 6+ = healthy diversification with broad participation.
dashboard.swarmDensityDeltaTip: Change in cluster tightness vs prior reading. Negative = clusters spreading apart (weakening conviction). Positive = clusters tightening (strengthening conviction).
dashboard.swarmHerdingTip: % of stocks in the largest behavioral cluster. >50% = dangerous crowding, momentum can snap. <20% = dispersed, no consensus.
dashboard.swarmInfo: Analyzes 50 large-cap stocks using DBSCAN clustering on momentum, volatility, volume, mean-reversion, and beta. Detects herding behavior: when stocks cluster tightly, the market has strong directional conviction. When noise is high, the market is confused. Score: -100 (extreme fear) to +100 (extreme greed).
dashboard.swarmNoiseTip: % of stocks with uncorrelated behavior (outliers). High noise = market confusion, no clear direction. Low noise = strong consensus, trend likely to continue.
dashboard.swarmTopFactorsTip: Features with highest variance among outlier stocks. These factors are driving the most disagreement in the market — the source of current uncertainty.
dashboard.title: Dashboard
dashboard.vix52wAvgTip: 52-week average VIX. Current VIX above this = above-average fear. Below = relative calm. The long-term VIX average is ~19-20.
dashboard.vix52wHighTip: Highest VIX spike in the past year. Extreme VIX spikes (>40) often mark capitulation bottoms — historically good buying opportunities for long-term investors.
dashboard.vix52wLowTip: Lowest VIX reading in the past year. When VIX is near this level, markets are unusually calm — good for selling premium, but complacency can precede sharp moves.
dashboard.vixInfo: The VIX measures the market's expectation of 30-day volatility on the S&P 500, derived from options prices. Low VIX (<15) = complacency, markets calm. High VIX (>30) = fear, heavy hedging. Spikes often mark short-term bottoms. Known as the 'Fear Index'.
dashboard.vixTermStructureTip: VIX term structure shows implied volatility across different time horizons. CONTANGO (normal): longer-dated VIX > short-dated = calm markets. BACKWARDATION (danger): short-dated VIX > long-dated = near-term fear spiking, investors paying up for immediate protection. Backwardation often precedes or accompanies sharp sell-offs.

models.empty: No quant model results yet. Click "Run Models" to generate predictions.

altman_zscore.label: Altman Z-Score
altman_zscore.long: A classic 5-ratio test on the balance sheet and income statement. SAFE (Z > 2.99) = healthy. GREY (1.81–2.99) = caution. DISTRESS (Z < 1.81) = elevated bankruptcy risk. Designed for manufacturers — banks and pure-tech can misclassify.

ensemble.label: Ensemble
ensemble.long: The final blended prediction. We weight the other models by current market conditions — in calm markets we trust momentum models more, in turbulent markets we trust fundamentals more. The percentage is the expected 3-month return. A forecast, not a guarantee.

factor_model.label: Factor Model
factor_model.long: Decomposes the stock's return into 7 well-studied drivers: market, size, value, profitability, investment, momentum, and quality. Tells you why the forecast is what it is — e.g. 'mostly a momentum bet' vs. 'pure market exposure'.

garch.label: GARCH(1,1)
garch.long: Does not predict direction. Answers: 'How turbulent will this stock be?' Reads annualized volatility: <25% calm, 25–40% normal, >40% turbulent. Persistence tells you how long a vol spike sticks — near 1.0 means turbulence feeds on itself.

kronos.desc: Transformer foundation model trained on 45+ exchanges
kronos.label: Kronos
kronos.long: An open-source Transformer foundation model (Kronos-base, 102M parameters) pre-trained on candlesticks from 45+ global exchanges. Reads the last ~400 days of OHLCV and autoregressively generates the next 63 days. Confidence bands come from 20 stochastic samples — wider bands mean the model sees multiple plausible futures.

lightgbm.label: LightGBM
lightgbm.long: Same idea as XGBoost with a faster algorithm and better handling of missing data. Confirms or contradicts XGBoost — if both agree, the technical signal is robust. If they disagree, the pattern is ambiguous.

lstm_forecast.label: LSTM Forecast
lstm_forecast.long: A recurrent neural network that reads the last 60 days of price and volume to predict the next 63. Uses attention to focus on the most important bars. Our confidence interval comes from running the network 50× with random neurons turned off — tighter interval = higher conviction.

mean_reversion.desc: How stretched is the price vs. its mean
mean_reversion.label: Mean Reversion
mean_reversion.long: Fits an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process and measures how far price has drifted from its long-run average, in standard-deviation units. z < -2 → statistically cheap (likely to revert up). z > +2 → statistically rich (likely to revert down). |z| < 1 → near equilibrium. Breaks down on strongly trending stocks.

monte_carlo.label: Monte Carlo
monte_carlo.long: Simulates 10,000 possible price paths using the stock's historical drift and volatility. The number is the probability of closing higher than today in 3 months. Above 55% = favorable odds, 45–55% = coin flip, below 45% = unfavorable.

piotroski_fscore.label: Piotroski F
piotroski_fscore.long: Nine yes/no checks on profitability, leverage, liquidity, and operational efficiency (each pass = 1 point). 8–9 STRONG (improving fundamentals), 4–7 NEUTRAL, 0–3 WEAK (deteriorating). A trailing indicator — tells you about past health, not future price.

price_predictor.label: Price Predictor
price_predictor.long: A simple linear regression baseline (Ridge/Lasso) on technical indicators. Acts as a sanity check — if the sophisticated models drift far from this simple one, the fancy forecast may be noise.

xgboost.label: XGBoost
xgboost.long: Tree-based machine learning that reads 40+ technical indicators (RSI, MACD, Bollinger Bands, moving averages, volatility, volume) and learns non-linear patterns from ~10 years of history. Outputs a 3-month return forecast. Only sees price and volume — blind to earnings and news.

optionsGuide.screenerTitle: How to find a trade with this screener
optionsGuide.screenerIntro: Two columns do the homework for you. Strategy is the system's premium-selling call — sell puts / sell calls / sell strangle — blended from the quant ensemble and the price-action read, with its conviction %. Best trade is the concrete balanced-profile idea: strike · days-to-expiry · probability of profit · annualized return. The table is still sorted by IV Rank (where options are richest vs their own year); the Verdict is the one arbitrated direction — read it first.
optionsGuide.sellTitle: Sell premium (income) — use the Strategy & Best-trade columns

sellSteps.s1: Sort by Strategy (conviction) or Best trade (annualized return). Favour names with IV Rank ≥ 70 (amber) AND conviction above ~50% — rich premium plus a real directional edge.
sellSteps.s2: Read the Best-trade cell: higher POP = safer (further OTM), higher annualized = richer. A 70%+ POP with a double-digit annualized return is the sweet spot; ignore thin-premium rows.
sellSteps.s3: Cross-check the Verdict: Sell puts wants a Long verdict, Sell calls a Short, Sell strangle a neutral / Conflicting one. If Strategy and Verdict fight, skip — the blend is uncertain.
sellSteps.s4: Click the ticker to open the chain and confirm: the suggested strike sits outside the expected move (±%) and behind a big open-interest wall, and the IV term structure isn't just a front-month earnings pump — trade past the event or skip.
sellSteps.s5: Plan the exit before entry — the Verdict card's invalidation level is the structural stop on the underlying; structure broken = close the short, don't wait. (Conservative and aggressive variants of each trade live on the stock's Options tab.)

buySteps.s1: Strategy / Best trade is a premium-seller's book; to BUY direction instead, look for IV Rank ≤ 30 on names with a Strong Long / Long (or Short) verdict — cheap options, clear direction.
buySteps.s2: Open the chain and compare the Verdict's target with the expected move per expiry: pick an expiry whose ±move actually reaches your target.
buySteps.s3: Buy a strike near the money (delta 0.45–0.60) — far OTM lottery strikes need the move AND the timing to be right.
buySteps.s4: Check theta: shorter expiries decay fastest; give the structural setup (weekly timeframe) at least 30–45 DTE.
buySteps.s5: Exit on the Verdict invalidation level or when IV Rank spikes (your option got expensive — sell it to the premium sellers).

optionsGuide.screenerFootnote: Strategy and Best trade come from the daily ranked book (balanced risk profile); conviction blends the quant ensemble with the price-action signal, and “—” means a low-volatility name the book skipped. Data is 15-min delayed (Polygon Starter). P/C OI above ~1.2 = put-heavy positioning; 25Δ skew = downside-protection premium; the Unusual column flags strikes with abnormal open interest worth inspecting on the chain.
optionsGuide.chainTitle: How to pick a strike & expiry on this chain
optionsGuide.chainIntro: Everything here is real market data (greeks, open interest, volume — 15-min delayed). Work top-down: direction → expiry → strike → exit plan.

chainDirSteps.s1: Take direction from the Verdict card above — not from the chain. Conflicting / Stand Aside means no options trade today.
chainDirSteps.s2: Read the IV term structure: a spike in one expiry marks an event (earnings). Decide deliberately whether you trade through it or around it.
chainDirSteps.s3: IV Rank chip: ≥70 favours selling premium, ≤30 favours buying it.

chainStrikeSteps.s1: The expected move per expiry (under the term chart) is the market's ±range — sellers go outside it, buyers need their target inside it.
chainStrikeSteps.s2: Use the OI bars and the OI-walls panel: big walls below spot = support (put-sell anchors); above = resistance (call-sell anchors / long targets).
chainStrikeSteps.s3: Greeks sanity-check: delta ≈ assignment odds for sellers (~0.30 is standard); theta is your daily cost as a buyer.
chainStrikeSteps.s4: Check Unusual OI — a fresh concentrated position at one strike is flow information; don't sell straight into it.
chainStrikeSteps.s5: Plan the exit before entry: the PAM invalidation level on the Verdict card is the structural stop for the underlying — option positions die with the structure.

heatmap.guideIntro: A treemap: each tile is one stock, its area is its market cap (or whatever you size by), its colour is the metric you choose. Tiles sit inside their group, and the group label carries the cap-weighted day change of everything in it.
heatmap.guideAxes1: Universe — the S&P 500, the Nasdaq-100, both, or only the names in your enriched book. A thin indigo ring marks book names when you view an index.

Every metric uses one of three scales: diverging red–grey–green about a midpoint, a single indigo ramp for magnitudes, or the verdict colours for states.

desk.title: Option desk
desk.subtitle: Candidates for selling puts and covered calls, graded rather than filtered. Two hard gates — solvency and liquidity — then a weighted score. Names that fail a gate stay on the list with the reason, so a thin top tier explains itself.
desk.error: Could not load the desk. The upstream analytics box may be unreachable — the screener will still work from cached data.

guide.title: How to read this desk
guide.intro: The edge being harvested is the volatility risk premium: implied vol usually prints above what the underlying goes on to realize. Everything here is in service of collecting that without being handed shares you did not want.
guide.gatesCsp1: Solvency — a name is only excluded when Altman classifies it as Distress. Assignment means owning the shares, so the gate asks whether the company survives, not whether it is cheap.
guide.gatesCc1: Solvency — a name is only excluded when Altman classifies it as Distress. You already hold the shares here, so the gate is about whether to keep holding them; a distressed name is a reason to sell stock, not to sell calls against it.
guide.gates2: Liquidity — strike open interest of at least 500 and an underlying above $10. Below that the quoted premium is not obtainable: on a $0.25 credit the spread can be 20-40% of the trade.
guide.gates3: Altman's grey zone is uncertainty, not insolvency, so grey names stay on the list and are scored down instead.
guide.score1: IV percentile (30%) — how rich this name's implied vol is against its OWN year. Below the 50th percentile earns nothing; you would be selling cheap.
guide.scoreCc2: Piotroski F-Score (25%) — the willing-to-KEEP-holding test. You already own the shares; this asks whether the name deserves the position at all.
guide.scoreCsp3: OU z-score (20%) — how far below its statistical equilibrium the price sits. Positive z earns nothing: selling puts into strength is what gets run over.
guide.scoreCc3: OU z-score (20%) — signed for this side of the trade: it rewards names extended ABOVE their statistical equilibrium. An extended name pays richer call premium and has mean reversion working for the position, so the call is likelier to expire and leave you holding the shares. Selling calls on a name sitting below its mean caps the recovery you are waiting for, and earns nothing here.
guide.score4: Annualized return (15%), capped at 40% — uncapped, yield alone ranks a 150%-annualized penny stock above every quality signal.
guide.score5: Margin of safety (10%) — the smallest weight on purpose. The DCF behind it is missing for 37% of the universe and is unreliable on high-growth names.
guide.score6: Where an input is missing the weight is redistributed, not scored zero — a measurement gap should not read as a finding.
guide.funds1: ETFs are in the book now. A fund has no issuer to go bankrupt, so the solvency gate asks a different question: whether the fund's STRUCTURE survives being held.
guide.funds2: Leveraged, inverse and option-overlay funds are rejected outright. A daily-reset 2X fund decays through volatility and a 0DTE covered-call fund has already sold the upside — assignment leaves you holding something engineered to grind down, so "happy to own it" can never be true.
guide.funds3: F-Score and margin of safety are marked n/a rather than missing, and dropped from the denominator. A fund is scored on volatility premium, dislocation and yield alone, so it is not penalised for failing to be a company.
guide.funds4: A greyed score with a percentage next to it means only that share of the applicable weight was actually measured — read it as a hint, not a rating.
guide.before1: Check the Earnings column. A print inside the contract's life is flagged red — that is the most reliable way to turn a premium grind into a gap loss.
guide.before2: For covered calls, resistance is the LOWEST of three independent reads: the nearest volume shelf above spot (where holders have basis and supply appears), the heaviest call open-interest strike (where dealer hedging pushes back), and max pain. Lowest, because a covered call is capped upside — being early is cheap and being late is what costs.
guide.before3: A dash in the Resistance column means the price has cleared all three. That is information, not a gap: there is no overhead supply, so a rally has nothing structural to get through. Sell further out, or do not sell the call at all.
guide.before4: Your strike must be above BOTH resistance and your own cost basis. The Covered calls panel joins your portfolio to these levels in your browser — your basis is never sent upstream.
guide.before5: Annualized figures assume a mid fill. The current market-data plan returns no bid/ask, so treat every return here as an upper bound rather than an expectation.
guide.before6: IV percentile is shown instead of IV rank throughout. Rank is a min/max statistic that one bad print flattens for a year.
guide.footnote: Nothing on this page places an order. It reads persisted daily data — no live chain fetches, no broker connection.

sizedBook.label: What fits in the book
sizedBook.qualifier: {count, plural, one {# position} other {# positions}} sized
sizedBook.lead: A ranked list implies you can take all of it. You cannot — every cash-secured put ties up strike × 100 until expiry, so the real question is which handful fit. Enter your collateral and the desk allocates it breadth-first (every name gets its first contract before any gets a second) under a per-name and per-correlation-bucket cap.

howTo.intro: Type the cash you are willing to tie up, then Size it. Nothing is ordered and nothing is saved — this is a paper allocation you can re-run with different numbers.
howTo.step1: <lead>Enter your collateral.</lead> Cash-secured means you set aside strike × 100 per contract until expiry. A $16 strike ties up $1,600; a $700 strike ties up $70,000.
howTo.step2: <lead>Read the four tiles.</lead> Deployed is what the book uses, Cash idle is what it could not place, Est. credit is the premium collected across every position.
howTo.step3: <lead>Check the bucket chips.</lead> They show concentration by what moves together, not by sector label — a chip turning amber means you are near the cap for that group.
howTo.step4: <lead>Then place the trades yourself.</lead> The desk never touches a broker.
howTo.outro: Without a number the desk stays a ranking. That is the honest default: which names score best is a different question from which ones you can afford, and only you know the second.

sizedBook.underDeployed: Only {pct}% of the budget is deployed — there are not enough qualified names to fill it today. That is a candidate-supply limit, not a reason to loosen the caps.
sizedBook.nothingFits: Nothing fits. Every qualified name is either unaffordable at this budget or blocked by a cap — see below.
sizedBook.nearCap: At or near the {pct}% bucket cap
sizedBook.unaffordable: Qualified but unaffordable: {tickers} — one contract alone breaches the {pct}% per-name cap of {cap}.
sizedBook.readingCaps: Caps in force: no name past {namePct}% ({nameCap}), no correlation bucket past {bucketPct}% ({bucketCap}), at most {maxPositions} positions. Change your collateral to re-run.
sizedBook.readingCredit: Credit is the engine's mid-price estimate. The market-data plan returns no bid/ask, so treat it as an upper bound. Caps are fixed fractional, not Kelly — half-Kelly on the settled sample is about 10% per position, and 284 overlapping trades in one regime is too thin to size against.

coveredCallBook.qualifier: {count, plural, one {# lot} other {# lots}} of 100+ shares
coveredCallBook.lead: Your cost basis stays in your browser — it is read from your portfolio with your own session and joined to the desk's resistance levels here, never sent upstream. Only lots of 100+ shares can be written against.
coveredCallBook.unavailable: Your holdings did not come back — the portfolio read failed, so there is nothing to write calls against.

coveredCallBook.noLevel: no level above spot in the stored data
coveredCallBook.floorIsBasis: Resistance sits below your cost basis — writing at resistance would lock in a loss. Your basis is the floor.
coveredCallBook.blocked: {tickers}: resistance sits below your cost basis. Writing at the resistance level would cap you out at a loss, so the basis becomes the floor — and a strike that far above spot may pay almost nothing. Holding the shares uncovered is often the better trade here.
coveredCallBook.reading: Resistance is the lowest of three independent reads — the nearest volume shelf, the heaviest call open-interest strike above spot, and max pain. A dash means the price has cleared all of them, which argues for a further strike rather than a closer one.

tradeJournal.label: Trade journal
tradeJournal.qualifier: {count, plural, =0 {none open} one {# open} other {# open}}
tradeJournal.lead: What you actually did, at the fill you actually got. Every premium figure elsewhere on this page is a mid-price estimate — logging real trades is the only way to find out how far off they are.
tradeJournal.signedOut: Sign in to log trades. The journal is private to your account.
tradeJournal.unavailable: Your trades did not come back — the journal read failed.
tradeJournal.empty: Nothing logged yet. Log a trade when you open one, then mark it expired, closed or assigned when it resolves — the journal works out the P&L, the return on collateral, and the annualised figure from the dates.
tradeJournal.assignedTitle: Net basis ${basis} — the option kept its credit, but you hold the shares.
tradeJournal.reading: The win rate counts only trades that resolved without assignment. An assigned put keeps its whole credit, so counting it as a win would push a wheel journal toward 100% while the account fills with underwater stock. Assignments are shown separately and judged on the position — spot against the net basis of strike minus premium.

form.fillNote: Premium per share, as filled — not the mid the desk quoted.
form.assignedNote: You keep the ${credit} credit, and now hold {shares} shares at a net basis of ${basis}. This will not count as a win.

assignmentBacktest.label: If I get assigned, can I live with it?
assignmentBacktest.lead: Five years of daily candles, {trials} simulated entries across {names} names. Strikes are inverted from delta using the volatility known at the time — no future information, and no option prices, so there is no profit figure here on purpose.
assignmentBacktest.unavailable: Could not run the backtest. The analytics box may be unreachable.

aria.worst: Worst 5 percent: fifth-percentile excursion past the strike
aria.hold: Return on assigned shares after 63 trading days

assignmentBacktest.finding: Entering after weakness barely changes how often you are assigned — <hl>{baseAssign} to {cohortAssign}</hl>. What it changes is what assignment feels like: shares recover within 63 days <hl>{baseRecover} → {cohortRecover}</hl> of the time, and their return goes <good>{baseHold} → {cohortHold}</good>. The cost is opportunity: that cohort is {share} of all entries.

glossary.summary: What these columns mean, and what this does not measure
glossary.assigned: Assigned — finished in the money; the shares change hands.
glossary.touched: Touched — traded through the strike at some point. It runs at roughly twice the assignment rate, which is the standard probability-of-touch relationship and a check that the model is behaving.
glossary.worst: Worst 5% — the 5th-percentile excursion past the strike while the contract was open. This is what position sizing has to survive, not the average.
glossary.recovered: Recovered — of the assigned trades, how often the shares got back above the strike within 63 trading days.
glossary.hold: Shares +63d — average return on the assigned shares, measured from the strike.
glossary.noProfit: No profit figure. Historical per-strike option prices were never stored, so a P&L here would be a model on top of a volatility guess. Strikes come from inverting Black-Scholes delta with a {vrp}× volatility-premium multiplier.
glossary.noFundamentals: No fundamental filters. F-Score and Altman are stored as current values only. Applying today's scores to a 2022 entry would select companies that turned out fine and make these numbers look considerably better than the strategy is.

assignmentBacktest.reading: Every figure above is a path fact measured from daily candles, not a P&L: the question it answers is whether the shares you would be handed are ones you could hold.
